title: Mass defect and binding energy; Time dilation and length contraction; Particles, antiparticles and classification; Specific heat capacity and latent heat; Temperature, internal energy, thermal equilibrium
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: P01-uk1#t3 term and clue written for the game; P01-uk2#t2 term and clue written for the game; P01-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; P01-1#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: N04-1#N.3b, T01-1#N.2, T02-1#N.3a, T02-uk1#N.7, N04-1#N.6, T01-1#N.5, T02-1#N.9, T02-uk1#N.10a, N04-1#N.8, T01-1#N.9a, T02-1#N.10, T01-1#N.11.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Meson
items.clue: Particle made of a quark and an antiquark, such as a pion.

items.label: Neutron
items.clue: Baryon with quark content udd, giving a total charge of 0.

items.label: Antiparticle
items.clue: Counterpart of a given type of matter, with the same mass but the opposite charge.

items.label: Positron
items.clue: Example of antimatter that comes out of β⁺ decay and is used in hospital PET scans.

questions.stem: Radium-226 decays by α emission: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂α. The atomic masses are 226.025410 u for radium-226, 222.017578 u for radon-222 and 4.002603 u for helium-4 (the electron masses cancel). Take 1 u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931.5 MeV c⁻², 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. How much energy is released in the decay of one radium-226 nucleus?

A 0.20 kg copper block at 80 °C is lowered into a large tank containing 200 kg of water at 20 °C. The water has far more internal energy than the block. Which statement describes the resultant thermal energy transfer?

options.text: From the block to the water, until they reach the same temperature.
From the water to the block, since the water has more internal energy.
Coldness passes from the water into the block, so the block cools down.
From the block to the water, until they have equal internal energies.

questions.stem: An electric kettle heats 250 g of water from 18 °C to 90 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. How much energy is transferred to the water? Ignore energy transferred to the kettle and surroundings.

A student finds the specific latent heat of fusion of ice with a heater in a funnel of crushed ice, but sets up no control funnel. The room is warmer than 0 °C. How does her value compare with the true value?

options.text: Too high, because some of the heater's energy escapes to the room.
Too low, because ice melted by the room is counted as melted by the heater.
About right, because the ice stays at 0 °C, so it takes in no energy from the room.
Too low, because the meltwater cools the heater, so it supplies less energy.

questions.explanation: Specific latent heat = VIt ÷ mass melted. The room adds mass melted but nothing to VIt, so the value comes out low.

questions.stem: Predict first. Which statement correctly describes the binding energy of a nucleus?

options.text: The energy released when the nucleus is separated completely into its nucleons.
The energy stored inside the nucleus, which it gives out when it later decays.
The minimum energy needed to pull the nucleus apart into separate nucleons.
The energy equivalent of the extra mass a nucleus has over its separate nucleons.

questions.stem: Sample P is warmed from 10 °C to 30 °C. Sample Q is warmed from 290 K to 310 K. Which statement about the two temperature changes is correct?

options.text: P's rise of 20 °C is equivalent to a rise of 293 K.
The changes differ, since kelvins and °C differ in size.
Both undergo the same temperature change, 20 K.
P's rise is larger, since P's temperature tripled.

questions.stem: 0.40 kg of ice at 0 °C is melted and the water is then warmed to 20 °C. Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹; specific latent heat of vaporisation of water = 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹; specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 × 10³ J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the total energy that must be supplied?

A student measures the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water. A heater keeps water boiling in a beaker on a balance. At 50.0 W, the mass falls by 6.0 g in 600 s. At 80.0 W, it falls by 14.0 g in 600 s. The rate of energy loss to the surroundings is the same in both runs. What is the specific latent heat of vaporisation?
questions.explanation: The losses cancel: specific latent heat = (80.0 − 50.0) × 600 ÷ (0.0140 − 0.0060) = 18 000 ÷ 0.0080 = 2.25 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.

questions.stem: Approximate binding energies per nucleon are: ²³⁶₉₂U 7.59 MeV; ⁹²₃₆Kr 8.51 MeV; ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba 8.33 MeV. A ²³⁶₉₂U nucleus splits into a ⁹²₃₆Kr nucleus, a ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba nucleus and three free neutrons. What is the energy change?

options.text: About 9.3 MeV is released
About 170 MeV is released
About 2.0 × 10³ MeV is released
About 9.3 MeV must be supplied

questions.explanation: After: 92 × 8.51 + 141 × 8.33 = 1957 MeV. Before: 236 × 7.59 = 1791 MeV. Free neutrons have no binding energy. 1957 − 1791 ≈ 170 MeV released.

questions.stem: You have 1.0 kg of ice at 0 °C and 1.0 kg of liquid water at 0 °C. Which statement about their internal energies is correct?

options.text: They are equal, since both are at the same temperature.
The water has more: its molecules have more potential energy.
The ice has more, since strong forces hold its molecules in place.
The water has more, since its molecules move faster on average.

questions.explanation: Melting takes in energy with no rise in temperature. That energy separates the molecules, raising their potential energy; their mean kinetic energy is unchanged.

questions.stem: 0.20 kg of water and 0.20 kg of cooking oil, both at 20 °C, are each supplied with 12 kJ of energy. Specific heat capacities: water 4180 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, oil 2000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Assume no energy is lost. Which statement about their final temperatures is correct?

options.text: The oil ends at 50 °C and the water at about 34 °C.
The water ends at 50 °C and the oil at about 34 °C.
They end at the same temperature, as each gets 12 kJ.
The oil ends at 30 °C and the water at about 14 °C.

questions.stem: A thermometer at room temperature, 20 °C, is placed in a cup of water at 70 °C. Its reading rises for a while and then stays steady. Why does the steady reading give the temperature of the water?

options.text: All energy transfer between the thermometer and the water has then stopped completely for good.
The thermometer then has as much internal energy as the water in the cup, so the two readings match.
The cold in the thermometer has then all flowed out into the water, so it can read correctly.
They are then in thermal equilibrium, so no net energy is transferred between them.
